title: Time-of-flight photon spectroscopy for scanning tunneling microscopy luminescence
authors: Lebin Yu, Jiří Doležal, Maximilian Rödel, Amandeep Sagwal, Benjamin Frölich, Martin Švec, Fabian Donat Natterer
abstract: We build and commission a time-of-flight photon spectrometer (TOFS) for scanning tunneling microscopy luminescence (STML). We obtain the spectrum by exploiting the wavelength dependent refractive index of a long dispersive optical fiber that converts photon arrival times into wavelength information; blue photons are delayed more than red photons. The setup uses a pulsed excitation source, either laser flashes or voltage pulses, to launch the photons from the junction into a single photon detector. The TOFS calibration can be performed and transferred to the STML setup from a separate benchtop experiment using pulsed light sources with known wavelength. We verify the TOFS during STML operation by simultaneously recording luminescence from the Ag-Ag(111) plasmon using a conventional grating spectrometer. Our experiments show that the TOFS is a straightforward and cost-effective addition to existing STML setups with good performance in the near-infrared range. The TOFS is compatible with a drop-in replacement of the single photon detector such as a superconducting nanowire single photon detector or even bolometers that may expand the useful spectral range beyond the abilities of current STML setups.
summary: The authors developed and demonstrated a Time-of-Flight Photon Spectrometer (TOFS) coupled with Scanning Tunneling Microscopy Luminescence (STML). This technique uses the wavelength-dependent delay in an optical fiber to measure spectra, offering a cost-effective alternative to traditional spectrometers. The method successfully validates spectral measurements in the near-infrared range by comparing results against established grating techniques.
main_problem: The primary goal is to obtain spectral information from extremely weak light emission sources, such as Scanning Tunneling Microscopy Luminescence (STML), while minimizing noise and complexity compared to conventional grating spectrometers.
main_result: The Time-of-Flight Photon Spectrometer (TOFS) was demonstrated to be a straightforward, cost-effective addition to existing STML setups, successfully reproducing spectral profiles in the near-infrared range.
method: Spectral analysis is achieved by exploiting the wavelength-dependent group refractive index of a long dispersive optical fiber, which converts photon arrival times into wavelength information via time-of-flight measurement.
model_or_system: The experiment couples STML (exciting plasmons on Ag(111) using voltage pulses) with a TOFS setup. The core physical principle relies on the dispersion relation within an optical fiber, where arrival times are measured by single-photon detectors.
key_observables: Photon arrival time ($	ext{t}_{	ext{transit}}(\lambda)$), wavelength-dependent group refractive index ($n_g(\lambda)$), and spectral intensity profiles compared between TOFS and grating methods.
important_parameters: Fiber length (up to 1000 m), pulse repetition rate, bias voltage/current for STML excitation, and the zero dispersion wavelength ($	ext{ZDW}$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes monotonic dispersion of the fiber material around the ZDW; discrepancies in intensity between TOFS and grating methods are attributed to uncorrected detection efficiency or attenuation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, raw arrival time histograms showing dispersion (red arriving earlier than blue), and direct spectral comparisons between the TOFS output and a conventional grating spectrograph using known features like notch filters.
paper_structure: The paper details the construction and calibration of the TOFS system using pulsed sources. It then validates this setup by measuring STML luminescence from Ag-Ag(111), comparing results against established spectroscopic techniques, and discussing limitations related to detector efficiency and timing artifacts.
why_interesting: This work showcases an advanced optical measurement technique (TOFS) applied to fundamental condensed matter spectroscopy (STML). The ability to perform high-resolution spectroscopy using time-domain measurements rather than traditional dispersive elements is highly relevant for quantum optics and low-light detection systems.

An arbitrary waveform generator, AWG (Ⅰ), is used to trigger electroluminescence from the STM junction in an ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) chamber, while a wavelength tunable laser (Ⅱ) is used for TOFS calibration. The TOFS setup, indicated by the dashed box, consists of a 50:50 fiber splitter (Ⅲ), which divides the photon stream into two optical paths. Figure 4: Voltage dependent photon spectroscopy of Ag-Ag(111) plasmon, as simultaneously seen by the grating spectrograph (orange) and TOFS. The shade encodes the excitation voltage added on top of a 1 V DC bias voltage, and the vertical arrows mark the onset of luminescence at short wavelengths.
